planting.note: Set divisions or plugs in spring into average, humus-rich soil at a woodland edge or clearing; this aster tolerates more shade than most of its relatives but still blooms best with a few hours of direct or filtered sun.

directions: Lindley's aster is a northern woodland-edge species whose heart-shaped, clasping leaves and lax, leaning stems distinguish it from open-prairie asters in the same genus. Loose sprays of pale violet-blue, yellow-centered flowers open in late summer into fall and draw a steady stream of bees and late-season butterflies at a time when many shade perennials have finished blooming. It spreads gradually from a short rhizome and is usually found along trails, thickets, and clearings rather than deep forest interior, so give it partial rather than full shade. Cut back old stems in late winter and divide crowded clumps every few years to keep flowering strong.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained woodland soil in dappled to partial shade; established clumps handle drier shade better than most native asters once rooted in.

directions: Drummond's aster is one of the more shade-adapted members of its genus, naturally occurring along wooded slopes and open understory where it receives only filtered light for most of the day. Its velvety, gray-green foliage and branching clusters of pale lavender to nearly white flowers appear from late summer into October, providing one of the few native nectar sources still active in shaded fall gardens. The arching, slightly zigzag stems give it a looser habit than sun-loving asters, so it reads best massed along a woodland path rather than staked upright. Divide every two to three years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom and keep the clump from thinning out in the center.

planting.note: Set nursery-grown divisions or plugs into consistently moist, humus-rich soil along a shaded slope or stream margin; seed needs a cold winter stratification and is slow to establish, so starting from an existing plant is much more reliable.

directions: Showy gentian is a southern and central Appalachian woodland species that favors moist, shaded seeps, stream banks, and rich cove-forest slopes rather than the open meadows typical of many bottle gentians. Clusters of deep blue-violet, fringed-mouthed flowers open in September and October atop low, leafy stems, giving a late burst of color just as most other woodland wildflowers are going dormant for the year. It is slow to establish and resents disturbance once rooted, so site it where it can remain undisturbed for several seasons before it reaches full flowering size. Keep soil reliably moist through summer, since this species does not tolerate drying out the way more open-habitat gentians sometimes can.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock into consistently wet, acidic, humus-rich soil at the edge of a shaded bog, seep, or stream; this species needs steady moisture year-round and will not persist if the site dries out in summer.

directions: Narrow-leaved gentian is a northeastern and eastern Canadian wetland species found in shaded bogs, fens, and streamside thickets where its narrow, grass-like leaves can be easy to overlook until the bottle-shaped, deep blue flowers open in late summer. Unlike the fringed petals of many showy gentians, its flower lobes stay closed or barely flare at the tip, a trait that distinguishes it in the field from the more familiar closed bottle gentian. It thrives only where soil stays saturated or consistently damp through the growing season, making it a good match for a shaded rain garden or bog planting rather than an average perennial bed. Leave the clump undisturbed once established, since gentians generally resent transplanting and recover slowly from root disturbance.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall into moist, humus-rich, acidic soil at a high-elevation woodland edge or shaded bald margin; this species is adapted to cool summers, so provide extra moisture and shade at lower, warmer elevations.

directions: Appalachian gentian is a high-elevation endemic of the southern and central Appalachians, naturally occurring along the shaded margins of grassy balds, spruce-fir forest edges, and rocky seeps from Virginia and West Virginia south into the Carolinas and Tennessee. Deep blue, bottle-shaped flowers with faintly mottled throats open from late summer into fall atop short, leafy stems, offering one of the last native nectar sources for bumblebees before frost. Because it is adapted to the cool, moist, high-elevation conditions of its native range, it performs best in gardens with reliably cool summers and consistently moist soil, and may need extra shade and watering to persist at lower elevations. Avoid disturbing established plants, since gentians in general reestablish slowly after transplanting.
